howto.name: Choose the subtitle file
howto.text: Drop or choose an SRT or VTT file, up to 4 MB and 10,000 cues. It is read in this browser and not uploaded. UTF-8 and UTF-16 files are read; a file saved in an older encoding needs saving as UTF-8 in a text editor first.

howto.name: Choose a translator
howto.text: On this device runs an OPUS-MT model in your browser: English into 19 languages, or 24 languages into English, with a model of about 107 MB for each pair that downloads once from Hugging Face and stays in your browser. Your own AI key sends the subtitles' text to the provider you choose and takes any pair of languages.

howto.name: Pick the languages
howto.text: On this device, choose the language the subtitles are in and the one to translate into; a file written in Japanese, Korean, Chinese, Thai, Hindi, Arabic or Cyrillic letters sets the first itself. With your own key, choose the language to translate into: the model works out the one the subtitles are in.

howto.name: Translate
howto.text: Click Translate. Consecutive cues are translated together as the sentences they form, then shared back across the same cues and wrapped to at most two lines of about 42 characters, or 16 for Chinese, Japanese and Korean. Every cue keeps its number and timing.

howto.name: Check and download
howto.text: Read each translated cue beside its original and correct any of them; cues that weren't translated, or that need a look, are marked. Then download SRT or VTT, named with the new language, such as talk.es.srt.

faq.a: Not to PrivaTools. The file is read in your browser. On this device the translation runs there too: what is downloaded is the OPUS-MT model for the language pair from Hugging Face, and the engine that runs it from jsDelivr, once. With your own AI key, the subtitles' text goes from your browser straight to the provider you chose, in numbered batches, and that provider's terms apply. Unless you turn analytics off on the Privacy page, Google Analytics receives an event saying the tool was used and whether it worked, never the text.

faq.q: Which languages work on this device?
faq.a: English into Afrikaans, Arabic, Chinese, Czech, Danish, Dutch, Finnish, French, German, Hindi, Hungarian, Indonesian, Italian, Romanian, Russian, Spanish, Swedish, Ukrainian and Vietnamese; and into English from the same languages except Romanian, plus Estonian, Japanese, Korean, Polish, Thai and Turkish. Each model works one way, so English to Spanish and Spanish to English are separate downloads of about 107 MB, and a pair without English, such as Spanish to French, isn't available on the device.

faq.q: Why does my own AI key handle any pair?
faq.a: A large language model reads and writes many languages, so it needs no separate model for each pair: it works out the language the subtitles are in and translates into the one you pick. It also sees the lines around each one, which helps with pronouns, gender and tone. Your provider bills you for what it translates, and a long film takes many requests.

Yes. Every cue keeps its number, or its VTT identifier, and its timing line exactly as written; only the text changes, and a timing is never changed to fit a longer line. VTT cue settings and NOTE, STYLE and REGION blocks stay too. Saving in the other format writes the timings in that format's style and leaves out what it can't hold, such as VTT's cue settings in an SRT, and the page counts what was left out.

faq.q: How are sentences split across several cues translated?
faq.a: Cues that form one sentence are translated together, because a fragment on its own is easily mistranslated or padded with invented words. The translation is then shared back across the same cues in proportion to the original text, breaking between words and preferring the comma or full stop where the original cue ended. With your own key, the model gets every line numbered and has to return the same numbers; a reply that doesn't match is tried once more in smaller batches and otherwise left untranslated, so no words are moved into the wrong cue.

It is a machine translation, so read it before you publish it. The on-device models are compact: idioms, jokes and names can come out wrong, and a short exclamation can be padded with invented words, so the page marks any cue that came out much longer than the original. A large model with your own key does better, but still makes mistakes.

faq.q: What happens to italics and other formatting?
faq.a: Formatting around a whole line, such as italics for a voice off screen, a position tag like {\an8} or a VTT voice span, stays around the translation. Formatting on a few words inside a line is kept with your own key when the model returns it intact, and otherwise left out; the page says how many were left out. Each translated cue is wrapped to at most two lines of about 42 characters, or 16 for Chinese, Japanese and Korean, and a cue that can't fit runs longer rather than changing its timing.

SRT and VTT files up to 4 MB and 10,000 cues, far more than a feature film needs. They have to be saved as UTF-8 or UTF-16: a file in an older encoding is refused rather than read with the wrong letters, so save it as UTF-8 in a text editor first. Subtitle Converter can turn ASS and SSA files into SRT. A timing line that can't be read stops the file, with its line number.

faq.q: How do I put the translated subtitles on my video?
faq.a: Upload the SRT or VTT next to the video where you publish it, or load it in your player; a name such as talk.es.srt lets players show the language. To burn the subtitles into the picture, use Add Subtitles, which uploads the video and the subtitles to PrivaTools for temporary processing.

faq.q: Can it translate subtitles from Subtitle Generator?
faq.a: Yes. Download the SRT from Subtitle Generator, open Subtitle Translator and choose the downloaded file.
